object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a given amount on a given cycle for a given product/plan.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: Unique generated identifier for a subscription, prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: One of the company's products, e.g. CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that says what the customer pays and how often; generates the invoice line.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: Code identifying a price plan, e.g. CORE-MO-49.

source_references.excerpt: CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: The feature bundle a customer gets -- seats, API access, SSO; the thing on the pricing page. Identified by name.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: Date a subscription starts; always present.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: Date a subscription ends; optional, present for fixed-term or cancelled subscriptions.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. ... A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The billing cycle of a subscription: monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual. ... Only those two.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The status of a subscription: trialing, active, past due, or cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

object_types.name: PausedFlag
object_types.definition: A separate boolean flag indicating a subscription is paused; not part of the status set, overlaps confusingly with active status.

source_references.excerpt: It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

object_types.name: PlanChange

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date a plan change takes effect.

ambiguities.description: Company name is explicitly rejected as an identifier for Account ('four accounts called Acme'), and email is on the contact rather than the account -- confirming account number is the sole identifier. This is not ambiguous, but is included here to confirm no composite identification issue exists. However, it's unclear whether 'Contact' (with email) should be modeled as a separate entity type since it's mentioned but not elaborated.

source_references.excerpt: Company name absolutely not, we have four accounts called "Acme." Email is on the contact, not the account.

ambiguities.description: The term 'plan' is used for three different concepts: the billing artefact (PricePlan), the feature bundle (FeatureBundle), and the sales-negotiated deal mentioned by Tom. The sales deal concept was explicitly deferred to a different meeting and is not modeled here -- should it eventually be captured as a distinct entity?

source_references.excerpt: So we've got two things both called plan. ... We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.

ambiguities.description: The 'Paused' flag on a subscription overlaps confusingly with the status field (a paused subscription may still show as 'active' status), and no constraint reconciling the two was agreed. Should paused be mutually exclusive with certain statuses, or is the overlap an acknowledged system bug?

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue) was explicitly excluded from the model as a derived/computed value rather than a stored fact. It is documented here for completeness but not modeled as an attribute or fact type, per the facilitator's explicit decision.

source_references.excerpt: So it's derived from the price plan and the billing period. ... I'm not going to model it as an attribute of the subscription, then, because it isn't a fact anybody asserts -- it's a calculation over facts we already have.

ambiguities.description: The commercial policy for mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions (run-to-term vs. prorated refund vs. credit) is explicitly undecided and parked by the facilitator. The model only captures the current system behavior (end date set to paid-through date, no refund mechanism), not any business rule about refunds/credits.

source_references.excerpt: What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided. The model will capture the system behaviour, which is that cancellation sets an end date and access runs to it, and it will not invent a refund concept that doesn't exist.

ambiguities.description: There is a potential redundancy/consistency constraint between the subscription's denormalised 'current price plan' field and the derived history from PlanChange records; when they disagree, the change history is authoritative and the current plan field is considered a bug. This is a data-consistency rule (subset/equality-like) that could not be cleanly formalized as a standard ORM constraint given the information provided -- should the model instead compute current plan purely from PlanChange history to avoid this discrepancy?

source_references.excerpt: Correct. And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: A fourth product is 'in discovery' but not yet defined or coded -- the product set (CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT) is fixed only 'today', suggesting the ProductCode value constraint may need to be revisited when the fourth product is finalized. No value_constraint was added to Product/ProductCode to avoid inventing/fixating a set that is known to be incomplete.

source_references.excerpt: Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: It is unclear whether 'RequestDate' (the date the change was made) is actually captured as a distinct stored field on PlanChange, or only implied conceptually alongside EffectiveDate; the transcript states 'we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates' but only explicitly lists 'the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it' as recorded fields (line 215), omitting an explicit 'request date' field.

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month. ... It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.
